title: AWS Operations Toolkit: Infrastructure as Code, Monitoring, Billing and the Well-Architected Framework
intro: Cloud operations on AWS is the set of services used to define infrastructure in code (CloudFormation, CDK), ship changes through pipelines (CodePipeline, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy), observe the running estate (CloudWatch, AWS Health, Systems Manager), control spend (Cost Explorer, Budgets, tags) and judge design quality (Well-Architected Framework, Trusted Advisor). The goal of this lesson is to give you a working map of these services, the exact questions each one answers, and the pitfalls that cause outages and surprise invoices, finishing with a guardrail baseline you could deploy for a new team account.

sections.heading: Why Infrastructure as Code, and the tool landscape
sections.content:
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means describing servers, networks, databases and permissions in text files that a tool turns into real resources. The alternative, clicking in the console, produces environments that nobody can reproduce exactly, review before they change, or roll back with confidence.

IaC gives you four properties that matter operationally:

- **Repeatable:** the same template creates identical dev, test and production environments, in any Region or account.
- **Versioned:** the template lives in Git, so every change has an author, a timestamp and a diff.
- **Reviewable:** a teammate approves a pull request before the change reaches the account, which is a control point that console clicks never have.
- **Recoverable:** a destroyed environment can be rebuilt from the repository, which is the foundation of disaster recovery for the infrastructure layer.

There are two broad styles. **Declarative** tools (CloudFormation, Terraform) describe the desired end state and the engine works out the steps. **Imperative or programmatic** tools let you write loops and functions in a general language; the AWS CDK is the main example, but it still produces a declarative template underneath.

| Tool | Language | Scope | State handling | Typical fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CloudFormation | YAML or JSON templates | AWS only | Managed by AWS inside the stack | Default choice for AWS-only teams, required by many AWS features such as Control Tower and Service Catalog |
| AWS CDK | TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, Go | AWS only | Synthesizes to CloudFormation, so state is the stack | Teams that want loops, types and reusable constructs |
| Terraform (or OpenTofu) | HCL | Multi-cloud and SaaS providers | State file you must store and lock yourself, often in S3 with a lock table or native locking | Organizations that manage several clouds with one workflow |
| Console or CLI by hand | None | AWS | None | Exploration only; creates drift and undocumented systems |

The most important concept to carry forward is **state**. CloudFormation keeps the state for you, so the question what does AWS think this stack contains is always answerable. Terraform needs its state file protected, because losing it or editing resources outside it breaks the link between code and reality.

The pitfall that unites all IaC tools is **out-of-band change**. Someone fixes an incident by editing a security group in the console, the code still says something else, and the next deployment either reverts the fix or fails. A mature team treats the console as read-only in production and uses IaC for every change, including emergency ones. The next section shows how CloudFormation detects exactly this situation.

sections.heading: CloudFormation in depth: templates, stacks, change sets and drift
sections.content:
CloudFormation turns a **template** into a **stack**, the unit of deployment. A stack is a named collection of resources that is created, updated and deleted together. If any resource fails during creation, CloudFormation rolls the whole stack back, so you never keep a half-built environment.

A template has these top-level sections:

- **Parameters:** inputs such as environment name or instance size, so one template serves many environments.
- **Mappings and Conditions:** lookup tables and if-logic, for example a larger instance only when the environment is prod.
- **Resources:** the only required section; each entry has a logical ID, a Type such as AWS::S3::Bucket, and Properties.
- **Outputs:** values other stacks can import, such as a VPC ID.

A minimal example:

```yaml
Parameters:
  Env:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, prod]
Resources:
  DataBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      Tags:
        - Key: env
          Value: !Ref Env
Outputs:
  BucketName:
    Value: !Ref DataBucket
```

Note DeletionPolicy: Retain. Without it, deleting the stack deletes the bucket. For databases and buckets holding real data, use Retain or Snapshot.

**Change sets** are the safety preview. Instead of updating a stack directly, you ask CloudFormation what it would do. The change set lists each resource with an action (Add, Modify, Remove) and, critically for Modify, a **Replacement** value of True, False or Conditional. Replacement True means the resource will be deleted and recreated with a new physical ID. For an RDS instance or an EC2 instance that is the line that tells you data or an address may be lost, so you stop and ask why before executing.

```bash
aws cloudformation create-change-set --stack-name team-baseline \
  --change-set-name review-142 --template-body file://baseline.yaml \
  --parameters ParameterKey=Env,ParameterValue=prod
aws cloudformation describe-change-set --stack-name team-baseline \
  --change-set-name review-142
```

**Drift detection** answers a different question: does the real resource still match the template? CloudFormation compares the live properties of each resource with the expected ones and reports IN_SYNC, MODIFIED, DELETED or NOT_CHECKED. Drift is the signal that someone changed infrastructure out-of-band. Not every resource type supports drift detection, so check the documentation before relying on it for compliance.

What to ask as an analyst or operator: Who ran the update, and was there a change set? Does any Modify show Replacement True? Is the stack drifted, and if so who changed the resource and why? Is there a stack policy or termination protection on production stacks? Remember that the API calls CloudFormation makes on your behalf run under the stack's service role, so the permissions of that role define the blast radius of any template.

sections.heading: Deployment and developer tools: the CI/CD chain
sections.content:
Writing a template is half the job. The other half is getting changes from a repository into an account the same way every time. AWS offers a family of developer services that chain together as a **CI/CD pipeline** (continuous integration and continuous delivery).

| Stage | Service | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Source | CodeCommit, or GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket via connections | Stores the code and triggers the pipeline on a push. Check current CodeCommit availability for new accounts; many teams use an external Git host with a CodeConnections link |
| Build and test | CodeBuild | Managed build containers that run commands from a buildspec.yml file, then discard the environment |
| Deploy | CodeDeploy | Rolls an application out to EC2, on-premises servers, Lambda or ECS using an appspec file, with in-place or blue/green strategies and automatic rollback on alarm |
| Orchestrate | CodePipeline | Defines the stages (source, build, approval, deploy) and moves artifacts between them |

A buildspec is a small YAML file that defines phases:

```yaml
version: 0.2
phases:
  install:
    commands:
      - pip install cfn-lint
  build:
    commands:
      - cfn-lint baseline.yaml
      - aws cloudformation validate-template --template-body file://baseline.yaml
artifacts:
  files:
    - baseline.yaml
```

The build runs under a **service role**, and that is the security-relevant fact. A pipeline that deploys to production holds powerful permissions, so anyone who can alter the pipeline definition or the buildspec effectively holds those permissions. Protect the source branch, require pull request approval, and scope the role to the stacks it manages.

**Deployment strategies** matter for reliability. In-place replaces the application on existing servers. Blue/green launches a new fleet, shifts traffic, and keeps the old fleet for instant rollback. Canary and linear shift a percentage of traffic over time. CodeDeploy can be wired to a CloudWatch alarm so a rising error rate triggers automatic rollback, which links deployment to the monitoring section that follows.

**Elastic Beanstalk** is the at-a-glance alternative for teams that do not want to assemble this chain. You upload application code (for example a Python or Java web app) and Beanstalk provisions the load balancer, Auto Scaling group, instances and monitoring, then manages platform updates. You keep access to the underlying resources, but it is a convenience layer, not a replacement for IaC at scale; its environments are themselves built on CloudFormation.

Questions to ask: where does the pipeline get its credentials, who can approve the manual approval stage, can a failed deployment roll back automatically, and are build logs retained somewhere searchable? A pipeline without an approval gate and tests simply delivers mistakes faster.

sections.heading: Monitoring with CloudWatch, and how it differs from CloudTrail
sections.content:
Amazon CloudWatch is the observability service: it collects numbers and text from your resources so you can see performance, set thresholds and react. Its main parts are:

- **Metrics:** time series of numbers, organized by namespace, name and dimensions, for example AWS/EC2, CPUUtilization, InstanceId=i-0abc. Many services publish basic metrics automatically; EC2 basic monitoring uses 5-minute periods and detailed monitoring uses 1-minute periods. Memory and disk usage are not collected by default; you install the CloudWatch agent to get them.
- **Alarms:** watch one metric (or a math expression) and change state between OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA. An alarm evaluates a statistic over a period, for example average CPU above 80 percent for 3 out of 3 periods of 5 minutes, then triggers an action: an SNS notification, an Auto Scaling policy, or an EC2 recover action.
- **Logs:** log groups and streams where applications, Lambda and VPC Flow Logs write text. **Logs Insights** queries them, and **metric filters** convert matching log lines into a metric you can alarm on.
- **Dashboards:** shared graphs of metrics and alarms for an at-a-glance view.
- **EventBridge (formerly CloudWatch Events):** routes events such as an instance state change to targets like Lambda.

A Logs Insights query to find the noisiest error sources:

```
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count() as errors by bin(5m)
| sort errors desc
```

The classic confusion is **CloudWatch versus CloudTrail**. They answer different questions.

| Aspect | CloudWatch | CloudTrail |
|---|---|---|
| Question answered | How is it performing right now, and is it healthy? | Who called which API, from where, and when? |
| Data type | Metrics, application and system logs, events | API call records (management and data events) |
| Typical example | CPU at 95 percent for 15 minutes | User alice called DeleteBucket from IP 203.0.113.9 at 02:14 |
| Action on data | Alarms, auto scaling, dashboards | Investigation, audit, compliance, detection |
| Time orientation | Near real time operational view | Forensic record of actions |

They work together. CloudTrail can deliver events to a CloudWatch Logs group; a metric filter then counts, say, root console logins, and a CloudWatch alarm notifies you. The detailed treatment of CloudTrail event fields belongs to the cloud audit logs lesson, so this lesson only uses it as the source for that pattern.

Pitfalls: setting alarms with no action attached (the alarm turns red and nobody hears it), treating INSUFFICIENT_DATA as healthy when a crashed instance simply stopped sending metrics (configure the missing data treatment as breaching for critical alarms), forgetting log retention (log groups keep data forever by default and cost grows quietly), and building dashboards nobody reviews instead of alarms that wake someone.

sections.heading: Health and operations: AWS Health and Systems Manager
sections.content:
CloudWatch tells you about your own workloads. Two other services tell you about the platform beneath them and give you safe ways to operate fleets.

**AWS Health** reports events from AWS that affect your account. It has two views:

- **Service health:** the public status of AWS services by Region, for everyone.
- **Your account health:** events specific to your resources, such as a scheduled retirement of the underlying host for an EC2 instance, an RDS maintenance requirement, an expiring certificate notice, or a deprecation of a runtime your Lambda functions use.

The operational move is to route Health events into your normal alerting. AWS Health publishes events to EventBridge, so a rule can send scheduled-change events to an SNS topic or a chat channel. Teams that only look at the dashboard when something is already broken miss the notices that exist to prevent the breakage. With AWS Organizations, an organizational view aggregates Health events across all member accounts so the central operations team sees them once.

A useful question set: is any resource listed in an open Health event, what is the action deadline, and does the affected resource sit behind redundancy so the retirement is a non-event?

**AWS Systems Manager** is a collection of operations capabilities that act on managed nodes (EC2 instances and on-premises servers running the SSM Agent). The ones to recognize:

| Capability | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Session Manager | Browser or CLI shell on an instance with no open inbound port, no bastion host and no SSH key; sessions can be logged to S3 or CloudWatch Logs |
| Run Command | Execute a script across many instances at once, with output collection |
| Patch Manager | Define patch baselines and maintenance windows and report compliance |
| Parameter Store | Hierarchical storage of configuration values and secrets, with versioning and IAM control |
| Automation | Runbooks (such as restart a service or snapshot a volume) that can be triggered by a person or an alarm |
| Inventory and State Manager | Collect software inventory and enforce a desired configuration |

The security benefit is real: replacing SSH with Session Manager removes an inbound attack surface and moves access control into IAM, where it is auditable. The instance needs the SSM Agent, an instance profile with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy, and a network path to the Systems Manager endpoints (internet egress or VPC endpoints).

Pitfalls: instances that never appear in Fleet Manager because the instance profile is missing, patch baselines that exist but are never attached to a maintenance window, and secrets stored as plain String parameters instead of SecureString. Together, Health, CloudWatch and Systems Manager form the loop: platform notice or alarm fires, an automation runs a documented fix, and the action is recorded.

sections.heading: Cost and billing: pricing fundamentals and the tools to watch spend
sections.content:
AWS billing follows three pricing principles: **pay as you go** (you pay for what you use, with no upfront contract for on-demand resources), **pay less when you reserve** (commit to usage for one or three years in exchange for a discount), and **pay less per unit as you use more** (tiered pricing, for example S3 storage becomes cheaper per GB at higher volumes). Data transfer into AWS is generally free, while transfer out to the internet and between Regions is charged, which is a frequent source of surprise. A free tier exists, but it is limited by time or quota, so a forgotten resource becomes a bill once the allowance is gone.

**Commitment options recap:**

| Option | What you commit to | Flexibility |
|---|---|---|
| On-Demand | Nothing | Full, highest unit price |
| Savings Plans | A dollar-per-hour spend for 1 or 3 years | Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda regardless of family or Region; EC2 Instance Savings Plans are tied to a family in a Region with a larger discount |
| Reserved Instances | A specific instance configuration for 1 or 3 years | Less flexible; Standard and Convertible types |
| Spot | Nothing, but capacity can be reclaimed with a two-minute warning | Deep discount for interruptible work such as batch jobs |

The tools:

- **Cost Explorer:** graphs and filters your historical cost and usage, groups by service, account, Region or tag, and forecasts the coming months. It also gives rightsizing and Savings Plans recommendations. This is where you ask why the bill rose in March.
- **AWS Budgets:** defines a threshold and alerts you. You can budget cost, usage, or the coverage and utilization of commitments. Alerts fire on **actual** spend or **forecasted** spend, to email or SNS, for example at 80 percent actual and 100 percent forecasted of a monthly limit. Budget actions can even apply a restrictive IAM or service control policy automatically when a threshold is crossed.
- **Cost allocation tags:** key-value labels such as team=payments and env=prod. A tag only appears in billing reports after you activate it as a cost allocation tag in the Billing console, and it is not retroactive; spend before activation stays unattributed.
- **Consolidated billing in AWS Organizations:** one payer (management) account receives a single invoice for all member accounts. Usage is combined, so volume discounts apply across the whole organization, and Savings Plans and Reserved Instances can be shared among accounts.

Pitfalls that cost real money: no budget at all, so the first alert is the invoice; untagged resources, which turns a cost review into archaeology; data transfer and NAT gateway charges nobody modeled; idle resources such as unattached EBS volumes and unused Elastic IPs; and buying commitments before usage is stable. A sound routine is to enforce tags through IaC, review Cost Explorer weekly grouped by tag, and keep Budgets alerting to a monitored mailbox rather than one person's inbox.

sections.heading: The Well-Architected Framework and Trusted Advisor
sections.content:
The AWS Well-Architected Framework is a set of design principles and questions for judging whether a workload is built well. It is organized into six pillars.

| Pillar | Core question | Example practices |
|---|---|---|
| Operational excellence | Can we run, monitor and improve this? | IaC, small reversible changes, runbooks, post-incident learning |
| Security | Is data and access protected? | Least privilege, MFA, encryption, logging, incident response plan |
| Reliability | Does it recover from failure and meet demand? | Multi-AZ design, backups, tested recovery, quotas awareness, health checks |
| Performance efficiency | Are we using the right resources for the job? | Right instance or serverless choice, caching, measuring before tuning |
| Cost optimization | Are we avoiding unnecessary spend? | Rightsizing, tags, Savings Plans, deleting idle resources |
| Sustainability | Are we minimizing environmental impact? | Efficient utilization, managed services, choosing efficient hardware and Regions, reducing waste |

The pillars create **trade-offs**. A multi-Region active-active design lifts reliability but raises cost and operational complexity. Aggressive cost cutting on a single instance lowers reliability. The framework does not give one correct answer; it makes the trade-off explicit so the decision is deliberate. The related Shared Responsibility Model decides which tasks are AWS's (the cloud itself) and which are yours (what you put in it), and every pillar question can be read through that lens.

The **AWS Well-Architected Tool** (in the console) walks a team through the questions for a workload, records answers, flags high-risk and medium-risk items, and tracks improvement through milestones. Lenses add specialized guidance, such as Serverless or SaaS. Reviews are most useful before launch and after major changes, not as paperwork.

**Trusted Advisor** is the automated counterpart: it inspects your account and reports checks in categories that map closely to the pillars:

- Cost optimization (idle load balancers, underutilized instances)
- Security (open security groups on risky ports, public S3 buckets or snapshots, missing MFA on the root account, exposed access keys)
- Fault tolerance (no backups, single-AZ resources)
- Performance (overutilized instances, large number of rules)
- Service quotas (usage approaching a limit)
- Operational excellence in newer check sets

A key practical fact: the full set of checks requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise support plan, while accounts on Basic or Developer support see a limited core set of security and quota checks. Treat Trusted Advisor results as a prioritized to-do list: each check shows status (green, yellow, red), the affected resources and a recommended action. It can also notify by email weekly and integrates with EventBridge for automation.

A short mapping habit helps in exams and in practice: a question about being able to rebuild an environment points to operational excellence or reliability, a question about idle resources points to cost optimization, and a question about who can reach a database points to security.

sections.heading: Governance at a glance: Organizations, Control Tower and SCPs
sections.content:
As soon as a company has more than a handful of accounts, the monitoring and billing practices above need a structure around them. Three services provide it.

**AWS Organizations** groups accounts under a **management account** into a hierarchy of **organizational units (OUs)**. It provides consolidated billing (one invoice, shared discounts), centralized account creation through an API, and a place to attach policies. A common layout separates accounts by purpose and risk: a security account for logging and tooling, a shared-services account, and separate workload accounts for dev and prod. Separate accounts are the strongest isolation boundary AWS offers, because a compromise or a misconfiguration in one team's account does not automatically reach another's.

**AWS Control Tower** automates setting up a multi-account environment following AWS best practices, called a **landing zone**. It builds on Organizations, creates a log archive and an audit account, enables organization-wide logging, and offers an **Account Factory** for provisioning new accounts with a standard baseline (often through CloudFormation or Service Catalog). It also applies **controls** (formerly guardrails): preventive controls implemented as service control policies and detective controls implemented as AWS Config rules, for example detect public S3 buckets or disallow disabling CloudTrail.

**Service control policies (SCPs)** define the maximum permissions available in the accounts they attach to. They never grant permission; they only restrict what IAM policies in those accounts could otherwise allow, and they do not apply to the management account. The mechanics and example policies are covered in the existing cloud security lesson, so use that lesson when you need the detail of writing a deny statement or testing its effect.

How the pieces connect to this lesson:

- **Billing:** Organizations gives the payer account one invoice and one place to view cost by member account; tags and Budgets then work at account or organization level.
- **Monitoring:** organization trails and centralized log accounts collect CloudTrail and CloudWatch data from all accounts into one protected location.
- **IaC:** Account Factory and StackSets deploy the same CloudFormation baseline into many accounts and Regions at once, so every new account starts with identical guardrails.
- **Well-Architected:** Control Tower controls are a practical way to enforce security and operational pillars at scale.

Pitfalls: running production workloads in the management account (which SCPs cannot restrict and which holds billing power), building a deep OU tree that nobody understands, and applying a broad SCP deny directly to the root of the organization without testing it on a sandbox OU first. A badly written SCP can lock out every administrator.

sections.heading: Worked example: guardrails for a new team account
sections.content:
A new team receives an empty account. Before they deploy anything, the platform engineer applies a baseline with three guardrails: cost visibility (an AWS Budget), a security detection alarm (CloudWatch alarm on root login), and consistency (everything is defined in one CloudFormation template). The team's CloudTrail already writes to a CloudWatch Logs group, whose name is passed as a parameter.

```yaml
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Team account guardrails baseline
Parameters:
  AlertEmail:
    Type: String
  MonthlyLimit:
    Type: Number
    Default: 500
  TrailLogGroup:
    Type: String
Resources:
  AlertTopic:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
    Properties:
      Subscription:
        - Protocol: email
          Endpoint: !Ref AlertEmail
      Tags:
        - Key: team
          Value: platform
  RootLoginFilter:
    Type: AWS::Logs::MetricFilter
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: !Ref TrailLogGroup
      FilterPattern: '{ ($.userIdentity.type = "Root") && ($.eventName = "ConsoleLogin") }'
      MetricTransformations:
        - MetricNamespace: Guardrails
          MetricName: RootConsoleLogin
          MetricValue: '1'
  RootLoginAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: root-console-login
      Namespace: Guardrails
      MetricName: RootConsoleLogin
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
      AlarmActions:
        - !Ref AlertTopic
  MonthlyBudget:
    Type: AWS::Budgets::Budget
    Properties:
      Budget:
        BudgetName: team-monthly-cost
        BudgetType: COST
        TimeUnit: MONTHLY
        BudgetLimit:
          Amount: !Ref MonthlyLimit
          Unit: USD
      NotificationsWithSubscribers:
        - Notification:
            NotificationType: ACTUAL
            ComparisonOperator: GREATER_THAN
            Threshold: 80
            ThresholdType: PERCENTAGE
          Subscribers:
            - SubscriptionType: EMAIL
              Address: !Ref AlertEmail
        - Notification:
            NotificationType: FORECASTED
            ComparisonOperator: GREATER_THAN
            Threshold: 100
            ThresholdType: PERCENTAGE
          Subscribers:
            - SubscriptionType: EMAIL
              Address: !Ref AlertEmail
```

**Explaining each guardrail:**

- **SNS topic:** the single notification channel. The email subscriber must confirm the subscription, otherwise alarm messages go nowhere. In production, point it at a shared mailbox or a chat integration, not a personal address.
- **Metric filter plus alarm:** CloudTrail is the source of truth that a root console login happened, and CloudWatch turns that record into a number and a notification. This is the CloudWatch and CloudTrail partnership from earlier. TreatMissingData notBreaching is correct here because no logins means no data points, which is the healthy state.
- **Budget with two notifications:** the 80 percent actual alert says you are close to the limit, while the 100 percent forecasted alert fires earlier in the month when the trend says you will exceed it. Forecast-based alerts need a few days of usage history to work.

**Deployment procedure:** commit the template, run cfn-lint in CodeBuild, create a change set for review, execute it, then run drift detection weekly. Enable termination protection on the stack, and activate the team tag as a cost allocation tag in the Billing console so the Budget and Cost Explorer can group by it.

**What this baseline does not cover:** it does not stop spending (Budgets only alert unless you configure a budget action), it does not prevent root use (an SCP or simply protecting the root credentials with MFA does that), and it does not replace a Well-Architected review. It is the minimum that guarantees someone hears about the two events that hurt most in a new account: unexpected cost and unexpected root access.

quiz.question: You run a CloudFormation change set on a production stack and see that an RDS instance shows Action Modify with Replacement set to True. What should you conclude and do before executing?

options.label: The database will be deleted and recreated with a new physical ID, so pause, check backups and ask why the property forces replacement
The database will be updated in place with a brief restart, so execute the change set during the next maintenance window
The template has a syntax error that must be corrected, because replacement only appears in failed change sets
The stack has drifted from its template, so run drift detection and then execute the change set to correct it

quiz.explanation: Replacement True means CloudFormation will create a new resource and delete the old one, so data or addresses can be lost. The right move is to verify backups or snapshots and find out which property change causes replacement. An in-place update would show Replacement False. Replacement is not an error indicator; syntax errors fail validation before a change set exists. Drift is a separate comparison between live resources and the template, and executing a change set is not a drift correction.

quiz.question: An instance's CPU has been above 95 percent for 20 minutes, and separately you need to know which user deleted an S3 bucket at 02:14. Which pairing of service to question is correct?

options.label: CloudTrail answers the CPU question, and CloudWatch alarms answer who deleted the bucket
Cost Explorer answers the CPU question, and Trusted Advisor answers who deleted the bucket
CloudWatch metrics answer the CPU question, and CloudTrail API records answer who deleted the bucket
AWS Health answers the CPU question, and Systems Manager answers who deleted the bucket

quiz.explanation: CloudWatch collects performance metrics such as CPUUtilization and can alarm on them, while CloudTrail records API calls including the caller identity, source IP and time, which is what identifies who deleted a bucket. Reversing the two services gives the wrong tool for each question. Cost Explorer and Trusted Advisor deal with spend and best-practice checks, not performance or API audit. AWS Health reports events about AWS services and your resources, and Systems Manager operates on instances, so neither one serves as the audit trail.

quiz.question: A finance lead complains that the monthly bill grew by 40 percent and nobody can say which team caused it, even though Cost Explorer is available. Which root cause and fix fit best?

options.label: Consolidated billing hides member accounts, so the fix is to disable it and give each account its own invoice
Resources are untagged, so the fix is to enforce tags in IaC and activate them as cost allocation tags
Savings Plans were purchased too early, so the fix is to cancel them and return to On-Demand pricing
CloudWatch is collecting too many metrics, so the fix is to turn off monitoring across all of the accounts

quiz.explanation: Without tags, Cost Explorer can only group by service or account, so cost cannot be attributed to a team. Enforcing tags through templates and activating them as cost allocation tags makes the spend groupable going forward, although it is not retroactive. Consolidated billing actually adds visibility per member account and shares discounts, so disabling it would hurt. Savings Plans cannot generally be cancelled and are not the reason spend is unattributable. Turning off monitoring would not explain a bill increase and would remove the visibility you need.

quiz.question: A team wants to be warned early in the month if spending is on course to exceed its limit, not only after most of the money is already spent. Which AWS Budgets configuration achieves this?

options.label: A usage budget on EC2 hours with a notification at 100 percent of actual spend only
A reservation budget that tracks Savings Plans coverage and alerts when coverage is above 90 percent
A cost budget with no notifications, then reviewing the Cost Explorer graph every Monday morning
A cost budget with a FORECASTED notification at 100 percent of the limit, sent to a monitored mailbox

quiz.explanation: A forecasted notification uses the current trend to predict end-of-month spend, so it can fire while there is still time to act. An alert on actual spend alone fires only when the money has been consumed. A coverage budget measures commitment utilization, which is a different objective. A budget with no notifications and manual review depends on human memory, which is the no-budget-alerts pitfall rather than a control.

quiz.question: During a design review, a team proposes a multi-Region active-active deployment for an internal reporting tool that can tolerate several hours of downtime. Using the Well-Architected Framework, what is the strongest critique?

options.label: It improves reliability beyond the stated need while adding cost and operational complexity, so the pillar trade-off is not justified
It violates the sustainability pillar because AWS does not allow a workload to be deployed in more than one Region
It is impossible to monitor, because CloudWatch metrics cannot be collected from more than one Region at a time
It removes the need for backups, which breaks the security pillar's requirement to encrypt every database snapshot

quiz.explanation: The framework asks you to weigh pillars against each other and against business requirements. Active-active across Regions raises reliability but also cost and complexity, which is unjustified when hours of downtime are acceptable. Workloads can be deployed in many Regions, so the sustainability claim is false. CloudWatch supports cross-Region dashboards and per-Region metrics, so monitoring is possible. Replication does not replace backups, and the encryption claim misstates the security pillar.
